results.summary_before: This project is a basic 8-bit CPU based on the SAP-1 architecture, using a 6-stage counter and LUT for control sequencing. It includes a program counter, instruction register, 16-byte memory, MAR, 8-bit ripple-carry adder with flags, accumulator, B register, and output register, all connected via an 8-bit tri-state bus. The design is tested by providing opcode inputs and verifying that the correct output bits are asserted. Notable features include support for conditional operation using carry and zero flags, and the design originates from a simplified educational CPU model.

results.summary_before: This project implements a DTMF (Touch-Tone) decoder that identifies telephone keypad tones using the Goertzel algorithm to perform a discrete Fourier transform. It accepts 8-bit audio samples at 44.1 kHz via a ready-valid handshake and outputs the detected row and column indices after processing 1024 samples. The design requires an external audio source and a clock of 50 MHz, and it uses a bit-serial multiplier that may introduce latency between samples. It is a specialized DSP application for decoding standard DTMF signals.

results.summary_before: This is a standalone VGA and sound demo that fits in two tiles, developed for the Tiny Tapeout demo competition. It generates a 640x480@60Hz VGA signal with a non-standard 1220-pixel horizontal resolution and RGB222 dithered graphics, plus 3-channel synthesized audio via a 16-bit sigma-delta DAC on a single pin. It requires a 48 MHz clock, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video, and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for sound. Silicon tests confirm both graphics and sound work as expected, matching FPGA simulations.

The design outputs the CPU register a0 and program counter bits for observation, along with test pass/fail signals. It requires only LEDs as external hardware.

results.summary_before: This is a software-defined radio core for AM reception that uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC and performs digital bandpass filtering and envelope detection. It is configured via a SPI interface to set the demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs a PWM signal representing the demodulated audio. External hardware includes a comparator, resistor bias network, RC network, SPI microcontroller, and an RF amplifier. The design is notable for its compact 1x2 tile size, trading off selectivity compared to a previous larger implementation.
